name: randomgen (NumPy-compatible bit generators: SFC64, Romu, Xoshiro256, PCG64, SFMT)
baseline: MT19937 as used by NumPy's legacy RandomState (also compared against MT19937, MT64, DSFMT inside randomgen)
workload: Time in ns to produce one random value (uint32, uint64, uniform double, exponential, normal, gamma) from each bit generator through the Python API, on Linux with an Intel Cascade Lake CPU at 3.1GHz.
claimed_speedup: uint64: Romu 2.6 ns, SFC64 2.6, Xoshiro256 2.8, SFMT 2.8, PCG64 3.2 versus MT19937 4.2 ns and NumPy RandomState 5.2 ns; uniform double: Romu 2.4, SFC64 2.5, Xoshiro256 2.7, PCG64 2.9 versus MT19937 4.0 and RandomState 5.2. The page's own overall geometric-mean score relative to RandomState: Romu(trio) 276%, Romu 268%, SFC64 259%, Xoshiro256 243%, SFMT 242%, PCG64 227%, MT19937 (via Generator) 191%.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (Family 6, Model 85, Stepping 7) at 3.1GHz, Linux
tradeoffs: Python/Cython package that needs NumPy; the C generator sources live in the repo and can be lifted into C/C++ projects, but the package itself is not a C++ library. SFC64 lacks jump-ahead (per the NumPy docs), so parallel streams rely on distinct seeds or Weyl increments; Philox, AES and other counter-based generators are available when many streams are needed.
caveats: First-party documentation table: CPU is stated but compiler and flags are not, and no benchmark script was located in the package tree. The page does not say whether values were drawn in bulk or one call at a time, so Python-layer overhead may be included. The legacy RandomState gap on normals and exponentials is inflated by Box-Muller and log-based inversion versus ziggurat in the newer code. The page itself recommends against all Mersenne Twister variants unless backward compatibility is needed. Baseline is NumPy's C MT19937, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/mersenne-twister and https://github.com/topics/philox topic pages (both list bashtage/randomgen); then the repo page and doc/source/performance.rst via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: NumPy numpy.random Generator (PCG64, PCG64DXSM, SFC64 bit generators)
baseline: MT19937 (legacy RandomState and MT19937 under Generator)
workload: Time in ns to produce one random value (32-bit and 64-bit unsigned ints, uniforms, normals, exponentials, gammas, binomials, laplaces, poissons) per bit generator, on Linux with an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X; plus relative tables for 64-bit Linux, 64-bit Windows and 32-bit Windows.
claimed_speedup: Uniforms: PCG64 3.1 ns, PCG64DXSM 2.9, SFC64 2.6 versus MT19937 5.9 and legacy RandomState 6.0; 64-bit unsigned ints: PCG64 3.2, SFC64 2.5 versus MT19937 5.6. Overall geometric mean relative to RandomState: PCG64 219%, PCG64DXSM 225%, SFC64 251%, MT19937 under Generator 159%. 64-bit Linux table normalised to MT19937=100: PCG64 161, PCG64DXSM 168, SFC64 192 overall.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Linux (main timing table); hardware of the Windows tables not stated
tradeoffs: Python-first API; using the generators from plain C++ means embedding Python/NumPy or copying the C sources. SFC64 lacks jump-ahead (per the same page); PCG64DXSM is recommended for heavily parallel use.
caveats: First-party docs: CPU stated for the main table, compiler and flags not stated. The same page shows the new generators are slower than MT19937 on 32-bit Windows (PCG64 25, PCG64DXSM 39, SFC64 77 versus 100) and Philox is 28 on 64-bit Windows, so the win is platform dependent. Much of the normals and exponentials gap versus RandomState comes from the algorithm (ziggurat versus Box-Muller or log inversion), not only the bit generator. The page does not say whether values were drawn in bulk or one call at a time. PCG64 is the PCG family already catalogued as pcg-cpp, so the PCG64 rows are evidence for that project as much as for NumPy.
found_via: GitHub: randomgen docs referenced NumPy's bit generators; opened numpy/numpy repo page and doc/source/reference/random/performance.rst via raw.githubusercontent.com (numpy.org itself was blocked)

name: simd-rand (SIMD Xoshiro256+ / Xoshiro256++ and frand generators for Rust)
baseline: Scalar Xoshiro256+ (benchmark label 'rand/Xoshiro256+', from the rand crate ecosystem)
workload: Criterion benchmark that generates and accumulates batches of u64x8 values (64 u64 values per iteration according to the page's Gelem/s figures) with scalar versus portable-SIMD and AVX-512 vectorised generators.
claimed_speedup: Scalar rand Xoshiro256+ 33.10 ns per batch (1.93 Gelem/s) versus portable Xoshiro256+X8 7.51 ns (8.52 Gelem/s) and AVX-512 specific Xoshiro256+X8 7.08 ns (9.04 Gelem/s): about 4.4x and 4.7x (derived from page data). The author's simpler 'frand' X8 generator runs 2.53 ns per batch, about 13x the scalar Xoshiro256+ (derived from page data). README text: vectorised PRNGs 'may perform anywhere from 4-6 times faster'.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile; Makefile comment says .cargo/config.toml sets target-cpu=native, AVX-512 builds use RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+avx2,+avx512f,+avx512dq,+avx512vl; rustc version not stated (nightly needed for the portable module)
tradeoffs: Rust crate (not callable from C++ without FFI work); the 8-lane generators produce eight independent streams per call, so the sequence differs from the scalar generator; lane jumps are not implemented (TODO in README); AVX-512 specific paths need avx512f and avx512dq, and the portable module needs nightly Rust.
caveats: The speedup compares the same algorithm scalar versus lane-parallel, so it measures vectorisation, not a better algorithm. Benchmarks keep the work observable by accumulating batches, which favours wide registers. The 'frand' generator is the author's own and the README says he is no expert in statistical testing; the latest commit is titled 'fix frand implementation (#34)', so frand numbers deserve a re-check. README warns old AVX-512 CPUs may throttle.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/xoshiro topic page (lists martinothamar/simd-rand); WebSearch 'SIMD vectorized random number generator AVX2 AVX-512 faster than mt19937 repository'

name: VectorizedRNG.jl (SIMD Xoshiro256++ for Julia)
baseline: Julia Base default RNG of the time (dSFMT-based MersenneTwister, a SIMD-oriented Mersenne Twister variant)
workload: BenchmarkTools minimum time to fill a Vector{Float64} of 1024 elements with randn! and rand! using the default Base RNG versus local_rng() from VectorizedRNG, on an old Haswell AVX2 machine and on an AVX-512 laptop.
claimed_speedup: Haswell AVX2 randn!: 7.235 us versus 3.744 us (about 1.9x, derived from page data); rand!: 791 ns versus 513 ns (about 1.5x, derived). AVX-512 (i7-1165G7) randn!: 1.676 us versus 854 ns (about 2.0x, derived); rand!: 549.9 ns versus 159.9 ns (about 3.4x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.6.0-DEV.1581 (2020-11-26), LLVM 11.0.0 (ORCJIT, tigerlake); JIT, no flags; benchmark snippets are in the README
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz (the versioninfo() printed after the AVX-512 run); the AVX2 run is only described as an 'old haswell machine'
tradeoffs: Julia-only (not usable from C++); 8 or 16 parallel xoshiro streams per thread depending on vector width, jump-ahead of 2^128 per stream; seeding is separate from Random.seed!; mixing vectorised and non-vectorised code can hurt performance.
caveats: Numbers are from 2020 on Julia 1.6 dev; the README says Base Julia used dSFMT only up to version 1.7, so the baseline no longer describes current Julia. The README itself says dSFMT 'in a few tests appears to outperform this library on AVX2 systems' for uniform numbers, and that the normal-distribution win comes mainly from a SIMD Box-Muller versus scalar ziggurat. AVX2 machine CPU model not given. Baseline is not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SIMD vectorized random number generator AVX2 AVX-512 faster than mt19937 repository' surfaced the repo; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Culumi PRNG (SIMD CLMUL-based 128-bit-per-step generator)
baseline: MT19937_32 (also SFMT19937, PCG64DXSM, xoshiro256**, xoroshiro128++, SFC64 listed in the same table)
workload: Table of time in ns per KiB of output for common PRNGs, fastest to slowest; separate BenchmarkDotNet table of Culumi versus System.Random methods.
claimed_speedup: ns/KiB: Culumi 58.68, Shioi 81.97, SplitMix 91.80, Seiran 97.26, SFC64 97.80, xoroshiro128++ 113.53, xoshiro256** 137.79, PCG64DXSM 308.30, MT19937_32 547.58, SFMT19937 953.13. That is about 9.3x faster than MT19937_32, 5.3x faster than PCG64DXSM and 2.3x faster than xoshiro256** (derived from page data). Against .NET System.Random: Next() 0.9371 ns versus 1.6193 ns (1.73x).
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12700F (stated for the .NET 8 BenchmarkDotNet table on Windows 11; the page does not say which environment produced the ns/KiB table)
tradeoffs: Needs x86 SSE4/PCLMUL/FMA for the C version; period 2^256-1 with jump functions of 2^128 and 2^192; 32 bytes of state; not cryptographically secure (state recoverable from three outputs with Z3 in a few hours per the README).
caveats: First-party README: the speed table gives no compiler, flags or benchmark code, and it is unclear whether the ns/KiB column was measured on the C or the C# implementation. No peer review. CC0 grants no patent rights (no patent grant). Latest commit is more than 3 years old.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Shioi128 PRNG andanteyk prng-shootout github' listed andanteyk/prng-culumi next to prng-shioi and prng-seiran; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Zest (generalized Ziggurat sampler: normal, gamma, Student t, etc.)
baseline: STL <random> distributions (std::normal_distribution and the other std distributions) and Boost.Random
workload: Approximate relative speed of generating variates from each distribution with Zest (1024 regions) versus the STL and Boost implementations.
claimed_speedup: Relative speed of Zest versus STL / Boost: normal 3.6 / 1.0, log-normal 3.1 / 1.0, Cauchy 4 / 4, exponential 3.3 / 0.67 (slower than Boost), gamma alpha>1 2.5 / 7, Weibull alpha>1 3.3 / 3.3, Student's t nu>1 10 / 20, Fisher's f d1,d2>1 6 / 11-14. README summary: 'faster than both STL and Boost in most cases, sometimes by a factor of more than 10'.
tradeoffs: Single header zest.hpp; GPL-3.0 copyleft; supports only unimodal densities; needs a URBG producing 32- or 64-bit unsigned values; table size (regions) must be a power of two and is a runtime/memory tuning knob.
caveats: Numbers are labelled 'approximate' in the README with no CPU, compiler, flags, standard library or URBG stated, and no benchmark code was found on the page; so this is first-party and unreproducible as written. Normal and log-normal are only on par with Boost, and exponential is slower than Boost. The README links an arXiv paper on the generalized Ziggurat which was not opened (arxiv.org is blocked here).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'ziggurat normal distribution faster than std::normal_distribution benchmark' (github.com only) listed DiscreteLogarithm/Zest; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: fastrand (PCG32 and xorshift128+ with nearly-divisionless bounded integers for Python)
workload: python3 -m timeit of a single bounded integer draw in [0,1001) or [100,1000] with fastrand versus random.randint(0,1000) and numpy.random.randint(0,1000).
claimed_speedup: fastrand.pcg32bounded(1001) 23.6 ns and fastrand.pcg32randint(100,1000) 24.6 ns versus random.randint(0,1000) 216 ns (about 9.2x and 8.8x, derived from page data) and numpy.random.randint(0,1000) 955 ns (about 40x, derived). README headline: 'up to 10x faster than random.randint'.
tradeoffs: Python extension with module-level generator state; pcg32 gives 32-bit output only and xorshift128+ is available only on some 64-bit platforms; not cryptographically secure; the C core (PCG32 plus Lemire's multiply-shift bounded draw) is small enough to reuse in C/C++.
caveats: One-line timeit measurements with no CPU, Python version or compiler stated; the gap is dominated by Python-level call overhead in random.randint and by its slower bounded-integer path rather than by raw generator speed. Baseline is CPython, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/prng topic page (lemire/fastrand, 124 stars); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: MRG32k3a branchless implementation (Vigna)
baseline: L'Ecuyer's reference double-based MRG32k3a.c (also the equivalent 64-bit integer implementation)
workload: Time to emit one double in (0,1) from MRG32k3a using the author's standard PRNG timing harness; output stream is identical to the original when seeded through MRG32k3a_init6().
claimed_speedup: Header comment: double-based reference about 17.5 ns per double, equivalent 64-bit integer implementation about 7.9 ns, this implementation about 4.1 ns (about 4.3x and 1.9x faster, derived from page data). README: 'roughly four times faster than the double-based implementation and two times faster than the trivial 64-bit integer implementation'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1 with the author's standard harness; optimisation flags not stated
tradeoffs: Single stream only (no stream or jump support yet); returns doubles in (0,1); emits the output from the current state, so one value must be discarded to line up with L'Ecuyer's original stream; state is six 64-bit integers.
caveats: First-party header comment with CPU and gcc version but no flags and no separate benchmark code (the harness is the author's external one, not opened here). The README itself notes that for batch generation nothing beats Intel MKL's vectorised MRG32k3a. Baseline is the reference MRG32k3a, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/pseudorandom-number-generator topic page (vigna/MRG32k3a); README, MRG32k3a.h and MRG32k3a.c opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: pgregory.net/rand (sfc64-based replacement for Go math/rand)
baseline: Go math/rand/v2 (PCG source and top-level functions), math/rand, golang.org/x/exp/rand
workload: Go benchmark suite (benchstat output) of Float64, Intn, Uint64, Shuffle, Perm, NormFloat64, ExpFloat64 and constructor cost, versus math/rand/v2 on a laptop and versus math/rand and x/exp/rand on a 48-thread Xeon.
claimed_speedup: Versus math/rand/v2 on i7-10510U: Rand_Float32 7.67 ns to 3.61 ns (-52.93%), Rand_Int31n 10.2 to 4.2 ns (-59.15%), Rand_Uint64 6.86 to 3.93 ns (-42.64%), Rand_Shuffle 711 to 412 ns (-42.12%), but top-level Uint64 3.06 to 3.20 ns (+4.75%, slower) and Float64 3.29 to 3.55 ns (+7.92%, slower). Versus math/rand on Xeon E5-2680 v3 with 48 threads: top-level Uint64 193 ns to 1 ns (-99.72%), Rand_Uint32 7.82 to 1.72 ns (-77.98%).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, linux/amd64; Go version and flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U @ 1.80GHz (versus math/rand/v2) and Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 @ 2.50GHz (versus math/rand and x/exp/rand)
tradeoffs: Go-only; deliberately omits the Source interface and top-level Seed(); generator is sfc64; Rand_New costs 48 bytes and seeding (Rand_Seed 46.09 ns versus 0.57 ns) is much slower than in math/rand/v2.
caveats: README author-run benchmarks without Go version or flags. The win over math/rand/v2 is mixed: raw top-level Uint64, Float64 and Intn are slightly slower than v2, and the headline gains are in float conversion, bounded ints, shuffle and the legacy math/rand package. The huge 99% gains versus math/rand are lock-contention effects of the global source on 48 threads. Go's own PCG source in math/rand/v2 is the closest named baseline.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/prng topic page (flyingmutant/rand, 240 stars); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: DualMix128 (128-bit-state PRNG; superseded by LoopMix128)
baseline: xoroshiro128++ (also wyrand, Java xoroshiro128++ and java.util.Random)
workload: ns per call of the generator in a 10-billion-iteration loop, built with gcc and run by benchmark.c.
claimed_speedup: benchmark.out: DualMix128 0.401 ns/call versus xoroshiro128++ 0.829 ns/call (about 2.07x, derived from page data) and wyrand 0.401 ns/call (parity). README: '107% faster than C xoroshiro128++, 27% faster than Java xoroshiro128++, 8.82x Java random'.
tradeoffs: Two 64-bit state words; period not guaranteed (README replaced the injectivity claim and points users to LoopMix128, which has a guaranteed 2^128 period); not cryptographic.
caveats: First-party; the benchmark output gives gcc version and flags but no CPU model. The repo is marked as replaced by LoopMix128, whose repository (danielcota/LoopMix128) now serves the biski64 README, and biski64 is already catalogued. Statistical claims: PractRand 256MB to 8TB with zero anomalies and BigCrush pass, per the README. Speed ties wyrand.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast PRNG library benchmark vs std::mt19937 header-only C++ xoshiro wyrand sfc64' (github.com only); README and benchmark.out opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: AVX512-VAES2-PRNG (AVX-512/VAES/GFNI 8-way hybrid PRNG, proof of concept)
baseline: Mersenne Twister (mt19937), PCG32 / XorShift128+, ChaCha8 and ChaCha20 AVX-512 (rows in the README table)
workload: Cycles per byte of bulk output on an AMD EPYC machine with AVX-512, VAES and GFNI, generating 64-byte outputs from an 8-way pipeline with non-temporal stores.
claimed_speedup: This implementation 0.0932 cpb (5.964 cycles per 64-byte output; best about 0.093) versus table rows ChaCha8 AVX-512 about 0.08-0.18 cpb, VAES about 0.16-0.20, ChaCha20 about 0.35-0.50, PCG32/XorShift128+ about 0.60-1.00, mt19937 about 4.00-6.00 cpb: roughly 43-64x versus mt19937 and 6-11x versus PCG32/XorShift128+ (derived from page data).
hardware: AMD EPYC (model not stated) with AVX-512, VAES and GFNI, shared server environment
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512 plus VAES and GFNI (recent Intel server or AMD Zen 4+ cores); outputs 64 bytes at a time; the author states it is not proven as a CSPRNG; the code is a single header.
caveats: Baseline rows are given as approximate ranges and are not shown as measured in the same run, no benchmark source or compiler flags are stated, and the more-than-50x gap versus mt19937 is implausible without flags, so the tier is capped at C. Statistical testing is thin: a SmallCrush-equivalent plus about 0.96 GiB of PractRand, and the author invites cryptanalysis and bare-metal benchmark contributions. Keep as a flagged proof-of-concept.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SIMD vectorized random number generator AVX2 AVX-512 faster than mt19937 repository'; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: zigg (lightweight Ziggurat normal, exponential and uniform generators with a C/C++ interface)
baseline: R's built-in RNG (rnorm, rexp, runif; base R default Mersenne Twister with inversion for normals)
workload: Chart from example/timings.R comparing zigg's zrnorm, zrexp and zrunif with base R equivalents.
claimed_speedup: README: speed gains of zigg relative to base R 'on the order of 7.4, 5.2, and 4.7 for the normal, exponential, and uniform' generators (for the author's example, on his machine).
tradeoffs: GPL (>= 2); C(++)-callable header-only interface demonstrated by four client packages; older, simpler Ziggurat generator with a shorter period than R's default, which the README itself says may suit only some studies.
caveats: The numbers sit in a chart image generated by example/timings.R; only the three ratios are given as text, with no CPU, compiler, flags or R version stated. The README also cautions that RNG time is usually a small share of total run time and recommends the well-tested R defaults for most uses. Baseline is R's RNG, not std::mt19937. The older sibling RcppZiggurat (GPL-2.0-or-later) has a vignette with a speed table that was not opened.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/ziggurat topic page listed eddelbuettel/rcppziggurat, whose README points to zigg; zigg README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: nanorand-rs (WyRand, Pcg64 and ChaCha for Rust)
baseline: Pcg64 as implemented in the same crate (port of rkern/pcg64); README also contrasts with PCG32 crates fastrand, oorandom, random-fast-rng and randomize
workload: Table of generator output speed in GB/s for each RNG shipped by the crate, footnoted as benchmarked on an M1 MacBook Air.
claimed_speedup: WyRand 14 GB/s versus Pcg64 1.6 GB/s (about 8.8x, derived from page data); ChaCha8 980 MB/s, ChaCha12 749 MB/s, ChaCha20 505 MB/s. README text: PCG32 crates are 'much slower than wyrand'.
tradeoffs: Rust-only; WyRand is not cryptographically secure and has a single 64-bit state; ChaCha variants provide the CSPRNG option; minimal dependencies and fast compile time are the stated goals.
caveats: First-party table with one footnote, no benchmark code, compiler version or flags. The Pcg64 figure of 1.6 GB/s (about 5 ns per u64) is far slower than PCG64 timings seen elsewhere (for example about 1.3 ns per value for pcg64_fast in the zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks README), so the gap mainly reflects this crate's Pcg64 port rather than PCG itself. The WyRand algorithm is the same as in wyhash (already catalogued).
found_via: GitHub: probed README of Absolucy/nanorand-rs as a Rust PRNG crate with a stated speed table; opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
